disclaimer: This is general guidance only and is not a substitute for advice from a qualified agricultural extension officer or plant pathologist. Local regulations and approved practices may vary.
description: Melanose is a fungal disease of citrus caused by dead and dying wood on the tree. It appears as small, raised, dark-brown or rust-coloured specks on the surface of fruit, leaves, and young stems. These specks often feel rough or sandpaper-like to the touch. On fruit, rain can wash the spores downward, creating characteristic tear-stain or mudcake patterns. Melanose does not affect the inside of the fruit, but it significantly reduces its market value.
immediate_actions: Prune out all dead and dying wood from the tree — this is the primary source of the fungus that causes Melanose.
Remove pruned wood from the grove immediately and destroy it; do not leave it on the ground.
Avoid overhead irrigation and any practices that keep the canopy wet for extended periods.
Do not handle or transport affected plant material to healthy parts of the grove.
Consult a local agricultural extension officer for approved treatment options if the infection is widespread.
spread_prevention: Carry out regular pruning to remove dead wood before the start of each wet season.
Disinfect pruning tools between trees to prevent mechanical transfer of fungal spores.
Improve canopy ventilation through pruning to reduce the moisture levels that favour the fungus.
Avoid wetting foliage and fruit unnecessarily during irrigation.
long_term_monitoring: Inspect trees for dead wood and Melanose symptoms regularly, particularly after storms or heavy rains.
Monitor young flushes of growth, which are most susceptible to infection.
Keep pruning records and track which trees show repeated infections — they may require more aggressive dead-wood management.
Discuss a seasonal management and pruning schedule with a local agricultural extension officer.
